reading.body:
Every tool in this category carries a regulatory burden that goes beyond standard software deployment, because healthcare AI touches protected patient data, attracts FDA oversight as a software medical device, or both.

Four of the five vendors operate under US jurisdiction, which means HIPAA governs how patient health information is stored, transmitted, and processed. Two tools explicitly require a Business Associate Agreement before a covered entity can use them at all. One tool handles genomic data, which falls under the additional protections of GINA. One is subject to FDA Software as a Medical Device rules, meaning its outputs can constitute regulated diagnostic claims. These are not compliance footnotes; they are hard preconditions that determine whether a deployment is lawful.

The one non-US entry, Insilico Medicine, is headquartered in Hong Kong and focuses on drug discovery rather than direct clinical care. The data flags cross-border data flows between Hong Kong and mainland China as a governance consideration, but it does not specify which regulatory frameworks apply or how that tension is resolved. That gap is meaningful for any organization evaluating the tool.

The data covers tool names, vendors, jurisdictions, and high-level risk flags as of September 2026. It does not cover pricing, clinical validation evidence, compute infrastructure requirements, or actual regulatory clearance status. Readers who need to know whether any of these tools holds an FDA 510(k) clearance or De Novo authorization will need to consult primary regulatory sources.
